title: Would You Let Yourself Be Fucked for Fifteen Euros? He Said
text:
"Would you let yourself be fucked for fifteen euros?" he said to me

at the bus stop at 0:42,

surrounded by empty, frozen streets.

First I shook my head, but then I told him:

Not for money, no, but if you vacuum and wash the dishes...

Then he, in turn, refused

and turned away dejected to continue on his way.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the Spanish verb's blunt sexual force and the poem's deadpan domestic reversal.

title: Dad, Yesterday It Rained
text:
Dad, yesterday it rained

and today it rained a little while ago.

Even so, it is warm.

A good mushroom autumn should come.


Dad, the evening news will be on soon,

and the sauna is ready.


Father, come back to my dream.

I will give you bread, cheese,

berries.

I will fetch water from the spring.


Dad, let me practice again.

It is strange to be so unfeeling.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the domestic invitations to the dead father and the final self-accusation.

title: He Had Barely Said: "Now All That Is Missing Is Strawberries"
text:
He had barely said, "Now all that is missing is strawberries,"

when I was already running toward the neglected garden behind the house

and had picked a handful of tiny wild strawberries

before he had finished eating his yogurt:

they had just ripened.

Be careful what you say, I said, now everything comes true.


And he was careful.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the magical domestic immediacy and the quiet joke of the final line.

title: Lovers Offer Each Other Kingdoms
text:
Lovers offer each other kingdoms,

new homelands, continents, and rare languages.

When they separate, the gifts remain with them;

they are irreversible,

and your love remains in them

as literature, language skills,

poems and stories

that they composed together

in each person's language.

Then love makes the world wider,

then, even in its disappearance,

it gives rise to peace and understanding.

New hearts open,

there is a little more to share

with the next lovers.
editorial_note: The translation keeps Kilpi's generous view of former love as an irreversible widening of language.

title: When One No Longer Has Strength to Write, One Must Remember
text:
When one no longer has strength to write, one must remember.

When one no longer has strength to photograph,

one must see with the eyes of the soul.

When one no longer has strength to read,

one must be full of stories.

When one no longer has strength to speak,

one must resonate.

When one no longer has strength to walk, one must fly.

And when the hour comes,

one must let go of memories,

of the eyes of the soul, stop dreaming,

fall silent and fold the wings.

But whatever happens, the narration goes on, goes on.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the repeated impersonal 'one' and the poem's insistence that narration continues.
